title: Day 43 · Week 6, Day 1 — Brain: the hormone she lends the brain — thyroxine, iodine, two big trials that didn't move an IQ, and the one line on the label
summary: The third Brain episode, picking up the line Day 36 ended on. Your baby is 4–6 mm at Carnegie stage 13; by stage 14 (~Day 45) the brain is about 50% larger, the velum transversum marks off the future cerebral hemispheres, the cerebellum begins as a thickening in rhombomere 1, the adenohypophysial pouch (future pituitary) is prominent, the first precocious neurons in the cord already send rootlets to muscle, and the thyroid is migrating down the neck but won't make hormone until ~Day 84 — so until then every molecule of thyroxine in the brain is hers (Morreale de Escobar 2004). Proof it crosses: cord thyroxine at a quarter to half of normal in newborns with no thyroid (Vulsma 1989). What the loan costs her: in 20 pregnancies on levothyroxine the requirement rose from week 5, median onset week 8, by a mean 47%, plateauing at week 16 (Alexander 2004) — a woman on levothyroxine raises her dose at the positive test (ACOG PB 223: ~25%). The cohorts: 7 IQ points lower in children of 48 untreated hypothyroid mothers, 19% vs 5% with IQ ≤85 (Haddow 1999, 25,216 sera); lower psychomotor scores at 10 months with lowest-decile free T4 at 12 weeks (Pop 1999, 220 women); an inverted U in 3,839 Generation R pairs — both low and high maternal free T4 at 9–18 weeks go with 1.4–3.8 fewer IQ points and less grey matter and cortex on 646 MRIs, while TSH predicts nothing (Korevaar 2016). The trials: CATS screened 21,846 women at 12w3d and treated 390 from 13w3d — IQ at 3 was 99.2 vs 100.0 (Lazarus 2012), and 101.8 vs 102.3 at 9.5 with a third of treated mothers over-replaced (Hales 2018); the MFMU trials randomised 677 women with subclinical hypothyroidism at 16.7 weeks and 526 with hypothyroxinemia at 17.8 — IQ at 5 was 97 vs 94 and 94 vs 91, neither significant (Casey 2017). Three ways both can be true, and the practical conclusion: ACOG PB 223 (2020) and the ATA 2026 guideline (Korevaar et al.) — test women with a reason, not everyone; repeat mild abnormalities before treating; treatment started after the first trimester hasn't been shown to help. Iodine: severe deficiency costs 12.45 IQ points and maternal iodine in pregnancy recovers 8.7 (Qian 2005, 37 studies, 12,291 children); mild deficiency in 1,040 ALSPAC mothers (median 110 µg/g) went with OR 1.58 for bottom-quartile verbal IQ (Bath 2013); 200 µg/day from 10.7 weeks in 832 mildly deficient women changed nothing at 5–6 years (Gowachirapant 2017); Cochrane 2017 finds nothing established for mild deficiency. The targets: 220 µg RDA, ~250 µg total (WHO, ACOG, ATA), a 150 µg potassium iodide line, never a sustained 500+, never kelp; US pregnant median urinary iodine 144 µg/L, 17.8% taking iodine, 34 of 59 prenatals containing it (NIH ODS). Food numbers; the sea-salt trap; the kale footnote. Three checks tonight: the label, the salt, and the levothyroxine call.
action: Tonight, three checks, two of them in the kitchen. One: the bottle from Day 33 — find the iodine line. If it reads 150 µg as potassium iodide, done; if there is no iodine line or it's under 150, buy either a prenatal that has it or a separate 150 µg potassium iodide tablet, and not a kelp or seaweed product however natural the front of the bottle says it is. Two: the salt. Pick up the container by the stove and the one on the table; if neither says iodised, buy a box of iodised table salt tomorrow and put it where the cooking actually happens. Three: the call. If your partner takes levothyroxine and the dose hasn't changed since the positive test, she calls the practice or her endocrinologist tomorrow morning, says she's six weeks pregnant and asks about the dose and a blood test. If she doesn't take it but her mother or sister has a thyroid condition, or she has type 1 diabetes or another autoimmune disease, write 'thyroid test — family history' as question nine on the Day 40 sheet, so it's asked with a reason instead of by default.
